shipped_rows.title_o: Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk

blind_target.evidence_quote: The General Social Survey (GSS) has conducted this experiment every other year since 1984; we use the 2014 GSS estimate as the baseline result.
blind_target.outcome_quote: This experiment behaves on Lucid much as it does on MTurk and the GSS – a large increase in support for redistribution when the question is phrased as assistance or caring for the poor rather than as “welfare.”
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors report agreement with the original experimental finding.

blind_target.title: The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) show that people take the riskier option when in a “loss frame” rather than a “gain frame.”
blind_target.outcome_quote: Lacking a US national sample benchmark, it is unclear how to grade Lucid’s performance relative to MTurk, though we would argue that the qualitative conclusions drawn from the experiment are the same across all samples.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors report agreement with the original experimental finding.

blind_target.title: Risk orientations and policy frames.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Our third experiment replicates Kam and Simas (2010), who show that risk acceptance correlates with choosing the risky option in an Asian Disease-type experiment, but that the treatment effect of the mortality frame does not vary appreciably with risk acceptance.
blind_target.outcome_quote: This finding was replicated in both MTurk and Lucid samples.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors report agreement with the original experimental finding.

blind_target.title: Through a glass and darkly: Attitudes toward international trade and the curious effects of issue framing.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Study 4 is a replication of Hiscox (2006), which measured the effects of positive, negative, and expert opinion frames on support for free trade.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Overall, the studies yield similar experimental estimates.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors report agreement with the original experimental finding.

blind_target.title: Rumors and health care reform: Experiments in political misinformation.
blind_target.evidence_quote: We attempted to replicate Berinsky’s 2017 experiment on belief in rumors surrounding the Affordable Care Act (ACA), specifically the false rumor that the ACA would create “death panels” that would make end-of-life decisions for patients without their consent.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Treatment effect heterogeneity for the healthcare rumors is also low for both the original Berinsky (2017) sample and for the Lucid sample (Figure 5). Treatment effects for all possible treatment possibilities are similar for both Democrats and Republicans for both samples. It is important to note that while we do not replicate the original ATEs for this study in the previous section, here we see that the CATEs are statistically differentiable for only Democrats receiving the Democratic correction to the healthcare rumor.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Direct comparison against identified experimental source; Berinsky average effects differ while heterogeneity agrees.

luna_triage.reason: The paper directly repeats the GSS welfare question-wording experiment in Lucid and compares it with the 2014 GSS estimate. The supplied article does not identify a specific published original paper for this recurring GSS experiment; the reference list's Gilens (1996) citation is specifically about race as a moderator, not established here as the source of the wording experiment. Expert scope/identity evidence is needed to decide whether the GSS series itself qualifies as the target original.
